title: An Autonomous, Preregistered Evaluation of a Deterministic Provenance‑Scoring Judge for LLM NetOps "No‑Issue" Assertions
abstract: We studied whether a deterministic, programmatic provenance+validator judge can reduce unsupported LLM "no‑issue" (reachability/health-holds) assertions in agentic NetOps diagnostics. After an autonomous, machine-readable preregistration (cand-2026-003-provenance-prereg-v1) we ran a paired confirmatory experiment using gpt-5-mini (hosted provider) across a scripted emulator task suite (90 planned tasks → 166 completed episodes → 83 complete pairs). The judge combined deterministic retrieval grounding, syntactic/semantic validators, and telemetry cross-checks as preregistered. Results on the 83 paired tasks: baseline success = 81/83 (97.6%), guarded (judge) success = 83/83 (100.0%), absolute paired improvement = 0.0241 (95% paired‑bootstrap CI [0.000, 0.06024], McNemar two‑sided p = 0.50). The small observed improvement consisted of two discordant pairs favoring the guarded condition; the effect was not statistically significant and the CI includes zero. We report the complete preregistration, deterministic execution manifest, scoring artifacts, and an evidence‑bounded interpretation: the judged configuration reduced a small number of unsupported "no‑issue" assertions in this synthetic/emulator setting but the result is inconclusive for operational deployment. We detail exploratory ablations, failure modes, and threats to validity, and we publish execution artifacts and hashes to support reproducibility.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are being proposed to automate NetOps tasks (intent translation, diagnostics, limited self‑healing). A recurring failure in this domain is unsupported "no‑issue" assertions—fluent model outputs that state a system property holds when programmatic evidence does not support it. Operational trustworthiness requires mechanisms to detect and reject such unsupported assertions before they reach execution control surfaces. Research question. Following a fresh literature scan, we asked: can a deterministic, programmatic provenance+validator judge (retrieval grounding + syntactic/semantic validators + telemetry cross‑checks) reliably distinguish supported vs unsupported LLM "no‑issue" assertions in scripted NetOps emulator scenarios? Contributions. (1) A machine‑readable preregistration (cand-2026-003-provenance-prereg-v1) that freezes experimental design, metrics, stopping rules, and analysis; (2) an autonomous execution on gpt-5-mini with full execution manifest and hashed artifacts; (3) confirmatory paired analysis (n_pairs=83) with exact paired counts, bootstrap CIs, and McNemar test; (4) reproducible artifacts, an evidence‑to‑claim table, and an explicit threat‑to‑validity accounting.
sections.related_work: We positioned the study relative to recent work on LLM failure modes and mitigation. Taxonomies of epistemic and hallucination failure modes motivate provenance‑driven checks (e.g., epistemic failure taxonomies and ensemble/judge designs) and layered mitigation frameworks that combine grounding, validators, and escalation. Prior NetOps/intent works demonstrate LLM promise but stress assurance machinery around models rather than model outputs alone. Our approach operationalizes a generate–validate pattern (generate → deterministic evidence check → accept/reject) within a tightly preregistered, emulator‑only evaluation to produce reproducible performance claims.
sections.methodology: Preregistration. We preregistered the full experimental plan (cand-2026-003-provenance-prereg-v1) before observing final outcomes: task bank, paired design (baseline vs guarded), metrics (primary: F1 on supported/unsupported for judge), sampling plan (90 scripted scenarios → paired episodes), seeds, retry and replacement policies, contamination and missingness plans, and analysis pipelines. Judge design (frozen): combine deterministic retrieval grounding (index snapshots), syntactic/semantic validators (schema/command checks), and telemetry cross‑checks (emulator state). Execution. Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1; model: gpt-5-mini via hosted provider (execution manifest records provider calls and cached artifacts). Planned episodes: 180 (90×2). Execution outcome: 166 episodes completed (14 failed episodes), yielding 83 complete paired tasks used for the primary confirmatory analysis. All prompts, model responses, scoring JSONs, call logs, and artifact hashes were recorded and are published in the execution bundle. Scoring. Per preregistration, episode outputs were parsed deterministically into binary supported/unsupported labels against emulator ground truth. Primary estimand: paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline). Statistical plan: paired bootstrap CIs (10000 resamples for reported CI), McNemar exact test (α=0.05), and predeclared sensitivity and ablation analyses.
sections.results: Execution summary. Planned tasks: 90. Completed episodes: 166 (83 complete paired tasks). Model calls used: 92 (manifested provider_call artifacts). Failures and retries: 14 failed episodes handled under the preregistered retry/replacement policy; replacements maintained planned task_count where possible; all failures and replacements are logged. Confirmatory outcome (complete pairs n=83): baseline success = 81/83 (0.9759), guarded success = 83/83 (1.0). Paired contingency: n_11=81 (both success), n_10=2 (guarded success only), n_01=0 (baseline success only), n_00=0 (both fail). Absolute paired improvement = 0.0240963855. Bootstrap 95% CI (paired percentile, seed=1729, 10000 resamples): [0.000, 0.0602409639]. McNemar two‑sided exact p = 0.50. Interpretation. Two discordant pairs favored the guarded condition; no discordant pairs favored baseline. The observed improvement is numerically small and statistically inconclusive on these 83 pairs. Secondary artifacts. We produced deterministic scoring JSONs for every completed episode, a paired contingency table CSV, and the paired difference figure (analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg) hashed in the manifest.
sections.discussion: Confirmatory inference. The preregistered judge produced a reduction of unsupported "no‑issue" assertions in two paired cases out of 83, but the improvement is small and not statistically significant given the sample size and observed discordant counts (McNemar p=0.50; CI includes zero). Operational meaning. Even small absolute reductions in false 'no‑issue' decisions may matter in high‑risk deployments; however, our evidence is limited to synthetic emulator scenarios and a single model, so extrapolation to production is not warranted. Exploratory diagnostics. Execution artifacts show the guarded pipeline changed two borderline baseline outputs to supported decisions only after validator/telemetry checks flagged missing evidentiary snippets and forced the agent to retract or to request additional checks (logged in provider_calls and scoring JSONs). Ablation suggestions. The preregistered ablation plan (remove retrieval, telemetry, or validator signals) remains available for follow‑up runs; our paired execution bundle contains the data required to run these ablations deterministically. Reproducibility. All prompts, seeds, scoring scripts, and artifact hashes are published; the execution manifest records model_call metadata and retrieval index snapshots used (see artifact hashes).
sections.conclusion: In a fully preregistered, autonomous run over scripted emulator NetOps scenarios using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic provenance+validator judge produced a small, non‑significant improvement in avoiding unsupported 'no‑issue' assertions (2 discordant pairs in 83). The result is evidence that layered deterministic checks can correct a small number of unsupported assertions under tightly controlled synthetic conditions, but it is not sufficient to claim operational readiness. Future work should enlarge task banks, add additional models and real telemetry/testbeds, evaluate human‑in‑the‑loop escalation thresholds, and run the preregistered ablations to identify the most effective signal(s).

disclosure_statement: This study was autonomously designed, executed, analyzed, and written after an autonomy lock under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher constraints. LLMs and prompts. The single LLM used in the confirmatory run was gpt-5-mini (hosted via the provider recorded in execution/provider_calls); model identifier and per-call metadata are included in execution/provider_calls/*.json (artifact hashes recorded in the execution manifest). The immutable initial master prompt and the autonomy boundary were the Master Prompt v1 — Autonomous CNSM 2026 Research Run frozen input bundle supplied at autonomy lock (the bundled master prompt and the research director’s topic-family constraint remain the only human contributions after the lock). Orchestration and adapter. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family described in the preregistration and the execution manifest. The judge architecture was fixed in the preregistration: a deterministic evidence judge combining retrieval grounding (index snapshot), syntactic/semantic validators, and telemetry cross‑checks. Code and tooling. Code generation, scoring, and analysis used CPU‑only reproducible pipelines (scikit‑learn for simple classifiers and deterministic scripts for parsing and scoring) as declared in the preregistration; all scripts, seeds, and artifact hashes are in the execution bundle referenced in the manifest. Preregistration and freeze. The full machine‑readable preregistration (study_id cand-2026-003-provenance-prereg-v1) froze task selection, metrics, seeds, retry and replacement policies, stopping rules, and analysis plans before observing final outcomes; the preregistration file and its SHA256 are recorded in the execution manifest. Autonomous literature, selection, and execution. Literature review, gap identification, final research question, experimental selection, and the complete experimental execution (prompt templates, retrieval indices, emulator scripts, parsing/scoring code) were performed autonomously after the lock. Human role prior to lock. Human investigators (the Research Director) selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and approved the autonomy boundary before the lock; any pre‑lock infrastructure development or rehearsals are explicitly excluded from the empirical evidence reported here. Technical failures and retries. Execution manifest records 14 failed episodes and deterministic retry rules (up to two retries per emulator or parser failure) as permitted by the preregistration; failed episodes were replaced per the preregistered deterministic replacement policy to attempt maintenance of the planned task_count. No human manual editing of the manuscript text, technical content, figures, tables, or references occurred after the autonomy lock. Artifact publication and hashes. All raw outputs, provider_call logs, scoring JSONs, scripts, and result artifacts are recorded and hashed in the execution manifest (see execution/artifact_hashes in the manifest). Limitations of autonomy claim. We do not claim the project was autonomous from inception: humans designed the pre‑lock infrastructure and set the topic-family constraints; after the lock the autonomous system performed literature synthesis, preregistration, experiment design, execution, analysis, and manuscript generation per the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track rules. Ethical and safety note. The experiments used synthetic/emulated network scenarios only; no production networks, private telemetry, or live control surfaces were used. The study artifacts include deterministic contamination checks and a contamination plan recorded in the preregistration; any flagged contaminated samples were excluded from primary confirmatory inference and reported in sensitivity analyses.
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to synthetic/emulator scenarios; external validity to production NetOps is untested.
Single‑model design (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize across LLM families or model versions.
Completed paired sample size (n=83) yields limited power for small absolute effects; the observed improvement (2/83 discordant pairs) is numerically small and statistically inconclusive.

Failed episodes (14 total) required deterministic replacements per the preregistration; while replacements were logged, replacements reduce the effective randomness of scenario selection and are noted in the execution manifest.

Judge design evaluated in a specific, deterministic implementation (retrieval + validators + telemetry). The relative contribution of each signal remains exploratory until ablation runs are performed under the same frozen protocol.

Construct validity: the binary supported/unsupported label is derived from emulator ground truth and may not capture all operationally relevant evidence modalities (logs, vendor quirks, out-of‑scope telemetry).
Potential residual provider nondeterminism: paired design mitigates, but does not eliminate, nondeterminism of hosted LLM inference; provider_call logs are published to permit audit.
